working_title: Electric or Push Trolley: How to Actually Choose the Right One for UK Golf
angle: Rather than a 'best of' product list, this post helps the regular UK walking golfer work out which type of trolley suits their actual situation: course terrain, car boot size, how often they play, and budget. The decision tree is practical and honest, not driven by upselling to the most expensive option.
research_notes:
- The core practical split: push trolleys require manual effort but are lighter, cheaper, and need no charging; electric trolleys use a battery-powered motor and remove the physical effort of moving the bag around the course
- Electric trolleys are naturally heavier than push trolleys due to added battery and motor components
- Push trolleys suit flatter courses and golfers who prefer low-maintenance simplicity; electric trolleys earn their keep on hilly or undulating UK parkland and links courses
- UK conditions (wet, hilly, soft fairways) are frequently cited as a genuine argument for going electric over push, particularly for golfers who play often
- Three key electric operation tiers: manual-steer electric (you still guide it by hand), remote-controlled (you send it ahead), and follow (it tracks you autonomously) — each tier costs more
- Lithium batteries are lighter and last longer than lead-acid alternatives; 27–36 hole range is common for mid-range lithium electric models
- 3-wheel vs 4-wheel: 3-wheel is more manoeuvrable on tight courses; 4-wheel offers better stability and weight distribution on slopes and soft/wet ground
- Downhill Control (DHC) or equivalent braking tech on electric models is a practical consideration for UK courses with pronounced slopes
- Push trolley frame materials: aluminium is the common choice for a good balance of weight, strength, and cost; some premium models use aerospace-grade aluminium
- Foot brakes are a useful feature on push trolleys for golfers whose home course has slopes or raised tees
- Handle height adjustment matters for comfort over a four-hour round — worth checking before buying
- Boot space is a real constraint: push trolleys fold smaller than electrics as a general rule, though some electric models have improved significantly on this
- GPS-integrated electric models remove the need for a separate rangefinder — a genuine consolidation benefit for the right golfer
- Folding mechanism quality varies widely; cube-fold and one-step fold designs mentioned as practical differentiators in the push trolley market
- Named models encountered in research (informational, no affiliate links unless approved): Motocaddy M7 GPS Remote, Motocaddy SE, PowaKaddy CT6, PowaKaddy CT10 GPS, MGI Zip X5, Clicgear 4.0, Stewart R1-S, Big Max Autofold FF, Motocaddy Cube Push, PowaKaddy Micra — mention only as illustrative examples, not as formal recommendations with links unless in approved-partners list
- Prices in research range from roughly £150–£200 for entry push trolleys up to £900+ for top-end GPS electric models — describe as general price tiers rather than citing specific figures that may change
must_avoid:
- No fabricated prices or specs beyond what research notes contain; describe price tiers in general terms if specific current prices are uncertain
- No affiliate links for any product not in /src/content/approved-partners.md; any named product not on that list must be mentioned informationally with no link, and no in-post note to the reader about this
- No personal anecdote implying the site owner has tested or owns any of these trolleys unless explicitly stated in a brief from a human editor
- No invented quotes from reviewers or brand representatives
- No medical or injury claims beyond generic advice (e.g. avoiding back strain is fine; specific physiotherapy claims are not)
- No financial advice framing around cost (describe price tiers factually; do not advise readers on whether they can or should afford a particular option)
- Do not duplicate the stand bag buying guide angle already published (what-to-actually-look-for-in-a-golf-stand-bag-for-uk-walking-golfers); this post is specifically about trolley type choice, not bag choice
- No em dashes anywhere in the post, including title and description
- UK English spelling throughout (manoeuvre, colour, favour, -ise endings)
